# Nudges and Choice Architecture {#sec-nudges}

Every choice a consumer faces arrives wrapped in a *context*: an order in which
options appear, a pre-checked box, a number printed on a label, a sentence that
frames the same outcome as a gain or a loss. None of these features alters the
underlying options, yet each reliably moves what people choose. A **choice
architect** is anyone who organizes the context in which decisions are made—the
designer of an enrollment form, the merchandiser who sets a shelf, the platform
engineer who selects a default. A **nudge** is any aspect of that architecture
that predictably changes behavior *without* forbidding options or materially
changing economic incentives. The defining feature is that the intervention is
cheap to avoid: a true nudge leaves the menu and the prices intact and works
through how the choice is presented, not through what is on offer.

This chapter treats choice architecture as both a scientific object and a
managerial instrument. Scientifically, nudges are where the behavioral-economics
account of the consumer—bounded rationality, reference dependence, present bias,
sensitivity to social information—meets the firm's ability to engineer the
environment. Commercially, the same levers that a public-health agency uses to
raise organ-donor registration are the levers a retailer uses to raise basket
size, and the line between a welfare-improving nudge and an exploitative "dark
pattern" is drawn by *whose* objective the architecture serves. We therefore give
equal weight to mechanism (why defaults, framing, social proof, and salience
work), to measurement (how field experiments identify a nudge effect and what
breaks that identification), and to ethics and welfare (when steering a chooser
is legitimate). By the end the reader should be able to formalize a nudge as a
shift in a choice model, design a field test that recovers its causal effect,
and reason explicitly about the welfare claim that justifies it.

The intellectual debt is to the heuristics-and-biases program—the systematic
departures from expected-utility maximization catalogued by @tversky1974 and
@tversky1981—and to the reference-dependent account of value in @thaler1985. The
managerial program that builds on it, **libertarian paternalism**, holds that
because choices are *never* presented context-free, the architect cannot avoid
influencing behavior; the only question is whether that influence is exercised
thoughtfully and in the chooser's interest.[^lp] We adopt that framing while
treating the welfare claim as something to be argued, not assumed.

[^lp]: The phrase is deliberately paradoxical: *libertarian* because options are
preserved and opting out is free; *paternalistic* because the architect arranges
the default to steer the inattentive chooser toward what the architect judges
better for them. Critics argue the paternalism is real and the libertarianism
partly illusory whenever opting out carries even small frictions—a tension we
return to in @sec-nudge-welfare.

## Theoretical Foundations {#sec-thn-foundations}

Choice architecture has no force of its own; it works only because human choice
departs from the rational-agent benchmark in regular, theorized ways. The
governing lens is **behavioral economics**, and each core lever in this chapter
is a deployment of a specific behavioral-economic theory. Naming those theories
makes the mechanism explicit and the welfare argument auditable.

The foundation is **prospect theory** [@kahneman1979prospect; @tversky1981]. People
evaluate outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point, with a value
function that is steeper for losses than for equivalent gains. This single idea
underwrites two levers at once. It explains **framing**: relabeling the reference
point (the "90% lean" versus "10% fat" contrast) changes valuation even though the
final state is identical, because the loss-averse chooser is not invariant to the
reference the way a final-wealth maximizer would be. It also explains the stickiness
of **defaults** through **status-quo bias**, the riskless-choice form of reference
dependence in which moving away from the inherited option registers as a loss and is
therefore resisted [@tverskykahneman1991loss]. The endowment effect (willingness to
accept exceeding willingness to pay) is the same asymmetry seen from the side of
ownership, and it is why a default, once held, feels costly to surrender.

Three further behavioral-economic theories complete the account. **Mental
accounting** [@thaler1985] holds that consumers code outcomes into separate,
non-fungible cognitive accounts, so the partitioning and framing of a cost (an
installment versus a lump sum, a fee versus a base price) changes evaluation even
when the net economics are unchanged. **Salience theory** [@bordalo2013salience]
formalizes limited attention: decision weights are distorted toward whatever stands
out in the choice context, which is exactly the primitive a salience nudge perturbs
(a calorie label, a conspicuous fee). And **present bias**, the hyperbolic-discounting
result that near-term outcomes are over-weighted relative to the long term
[@laibson1997hyperbolic], explains why people under-save, procrastinate cancellation,
and impulse-buy: it is the time-preference failure that automatic enrollment and
commitment-style nudges are designed to correct. **Social norms** supply the final
primitive: descriptive and injunctive norms move behavior, often more than people
predict, which is the engine of every social-proof nudge [@cialdini1990;
@goldstein2008norms].

These theories are organized into a managerial program by **libertarian
paternalism**, the framing introduced in Thaler and Sunstein's *Nudge*: because
choice is never presented context-free, the architect cannot avoid influencing
behavior, so the only question is whether that influence is exercised thoughtfully
and in the chooser's interest. The program's empirical credibility rests on field
evidence that defaults and reminders change behavior cheaply at scale
[@johnson2003defaults; @benartzi2017nudging]. Its critics press two objections. The
first is normative: the paternalism is real, and the "libertarian" promise of a free
opt-out is partly illusory wherever exiting carries even small friction, the concern
formalized as **sludge**, the welfare-reducing mirror of a nudge [@thaler2018sludge].
The second is empirical: meta-analytic re-readings argue that average nudge effects
are smaller and more publication-biased than the headline cases suggest, so the
intervention should be sized honestly rather than oversold. We adopt the
libertarian-paternalism framing while treating both the welfare claim and the effect
size as quantities to be argued and measured, not assumed; @sec-nudge-welfare and
@sec-nudge-identification take up each in turn.

## What a Nudge Is, Formally

Intuitively, a nudge changes behavior without changing the rational consumer's
problem. To make this precise, consider a chooser selecting from a menu
$\mathcal{C} = \{1,\dots,J\}$ of options, each with attributes
$\mathbf{x}_j$ and price $p_j$. In the standard random-utility model the chooser
selects option $j$ when its latent utility is largest,
$$
U_j = V(\mathbf{x}_j, p_j) + \varepsilon_j, \qquad
j^\star = \arg\max_{j \in \mathcal{C}} U_j ,
$$ {#eq-16-rum}
with $V$ the deterministic (systematic) component and $\varepsilon_j$ an
idiosyncratic shock. A *price cut* or a *quality improvement* moves choices by
changing $V$ through $p_j$ or $\mathbf{x}_j$. A *ban* moves choices by deleting
$j$ from $\mathcal{C}$. A **nudge does neither.** It is a feature $a$ of the
choice architecture that enters utility (or the choice rule) without changing the
menu $\mathcal{C}$ or the economic terms $(\mathbf{x}_j, p_j)$:
$$
\tilde U_j = V(\mathbf{x}_j, p_j) + \gamma\, d_j(a) + \varepsilon_j ,
$$ {#eq-nudge}
where $d_j(a)$ encodes how architecture $a$ touches option $j$—an indicator that
$j$ is the default, the rank of $j$ in a list, the salience weight on $j$'s
price—and $\gamma$ is the behavioral sensitivity. Under the neoclassical axioms
$\gamma = 0$: presentation is irrelevant and choice is invariant to anything but
$(\mathbf{x}_j, p_j)$. Every nudge is, in this notation, a claim that
$\gamma \neq 0$ for some architecture-dependent term that a fully rational agent
would ignore. @fig-nud-formal locates the nudge among the interventions available
to anyone who shapes a choice: it alone moves behavior while leaving both the menu
and the economic terms intact.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-nud-formal
%%| fig-cap: "Three ways to move a choice, and what each changes. A price cut or quality improvement works through the economic terms; a ban works through the menu; a nudge changes neither, entering utility only through an architecture term that a fully rational chooser would ignore."
flowchart TD
  I["Intervention on a choice from<br/>menu C with attributes x_j<br/>and prices p_j"] --> PC["Price cut or<br/>quality improvement"]
  I --> BN["Ban"]
  I --> ND["Nudge"]
  PC --> PC2["Changes V through<br/>p_j or x_j:<br/>economic incentives"]
  BN --> BN2["Deletes option j<br/>from the menu C"]
  ND --> ND2["Adds γ·d_j(a):<br/>default status, list rank,<br/>salience weight"]
  ND2 --> ND3["Menu and prices intact;<br/>under neoclassical axioms γ = 0"]
```

> A **nudge** is any aspect of the choice architecture that alters people's
> behavior in a predictable way without forbidding any options or significantly
> changing their economic incentives. To count as a mere nudge, the intervention
> must be easy and cheap to avoid.
>
> --- after the standard definition in the libertarian-paternalism literature

Two corollaries follow and discipline the rest of the chapter. First, because the
nudge operates through $\gamma\, d_j(a)$ rather than through preferences, its
effect is a property of the *interaction* between the architecture and the
population's behavioral parameters—the same default can be inert in one segment
and decisive in another (@sec-nudge-heterogeneity). Second, the welfare
evaluation of a nudge cannot be read off revealed choice in the usual way:
if $\gamma \neq 0$, the option chosen under architecture $a$ need not be the one
that maximizes the chooser's *experienced* utility, so the architect must invoke
a welfare criterion external to the choice itself (@sec-nudge-welfare).

It is useful to separate two channels by which $d_j(a)$ can act, because they
imply different robustness and different ethics. A nudge may **supply
information or structure** that a rational but cognitively limited agent would
want—reducing search cost, correcting a misperception, making a consequence
vivid—in which case it moves choice toward what the agent would pick on
reflection. Or it may **exploit a bias**—anchoring on an arbitrary number,
triggering loss aversion, leveraging inertia—in which case it moves choice
toward what the architect wants regardless of the chooser's interest. The same
formal object, $\gamma\, d_j(a)$, covers both; the welfare sign is not in the
math but in the mapping from the manipulated choice to the chooser's own ends.

Even within the bias-exploiting channel, force is not guaranteed. The
arbitrary-number anchoring that folklore treats as universal is, across fifty years
of evidence, among the *weakest* forms: meta-analyzing more than 2,600 effect sizes,
@schley2026anchoring find that incidental and random-number anchors show much smaller
and sometimes null effects once incentives or debiasing enter, while informative
anchors stay robust (Hedges' $g \approx 0.83$). Naming a mechanism does not certify
that a nudge will move anyone—an empirical caution the boundary-conditions discussion
later in the chapter develops.

::: callout-note
## Controversy: how big is a nudge, really?

The aggregate effectiveness of choice architecture has been contested in print since
2022, and the dispute is as much about meta-analytic method as about nudges. It is a
useful case precisely because all parties are looking at overlapping evidence.

**2022 — the pooled estimate.** @mertens2022nudging publish *The Effectiveness of
Nudging: A Meta-Analysis of Choice Architecture Interventions Across Behavioral Domains*
in *PNAS*, reporting a moderate positive average effect.

**2022 — two reanalyses, same journal, same year.** The replies do not bury their
conclusions in the abstract. @maier2022nonudge is titled *No Evidence for Nudging After
Adjusting for Publication Bias*: reanalyzing the same evidence with bias corrections,
they report an average effect not distinguishable from zero. @szaszi2022noexpect is
titled *No Reason to Expect Large and Consistent Effects of Nudge Interventions*, and
raises a different objection—the heterogeneity across interventions is so large that a
pooled average is not the right summary object at all.

Three papers, one journal, one year, and the disagreement stated in the titles. This is
the fastest published exchange in the set of controversies this book documents, and the
speed is a function of format: *PNAS* accommodates short letters, so a reanalysis can
appear while the original is still news, rather than the decade-long lags typical of the
marketing exchanges in @sec-cred-public-argument.

**Where it rests.** These are not reconcilable by collecting more studies, because the
disagreement is about what to do with the studies already collected—specifically, how
aggressively to correct for the fact that null nudge results are less likely to be
published, and whether averaging across heterogeneous interventions produces a number
that means anything. Both are live methodological questions in every applied
meta-analysis, not just this one.

The practical reading for someone designing a nudge is that neither "nudges work" nor
"nudges do not work" is a claim the evidence supports at that level of generality. The
useful questions are which lever, in which population, against which baseline—which is
how the rest of this chapter is organized. @sec-cred-crisis places this exchange within
the broader credibility revolution, and @sec-satisfaction-meta shows the same
base-rate reasoning applied to a different literature.
:::

## The Core Levers

Four families of nudge recur across domains because each maps onto a robust
regularity in how people depart from @eq-16-rum. @tbl-levers organizes them by the
behavioral primitive each exploits, the formal object it perturbs, and the
canonical field application. We then treat each in turn.

| Lever | Behavioral primitive | What it perturbs in @eq-nudge | Canonical application |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Default** | Status-quo bias, inertia, effort cost | Sets $d_j(a)=1$ for the opt-out option | Auto-enrollment in retirement saving; organ donation |
| **Framing** | Reference dependence, loss aversion | Relabels the *reference point* in $V$ | "90% lean" vs. "10% fat"; gain/loss appeals |
| **Social proof** | Conformity, descriptive norms | Adds a term in others' choices to $V$ | "Most guests reuse their towels"; energy reports |
| **Salience** | Limited attention, fluency | Reweights an attribute already in $V$ | Calorie labels; "sale" tags; traffic-light nutrition |

: Four core nudge levers, the behavioral primitive each exploits, and where each enters the choice model. {#tbl-levers}

### Defaults

A **default** is the outcome that obtains when the chooser does nothing. Defaults
are the most powerful nudge because doing nothing is the cheapest action: any
positive cost of deliberation, comprehension, or execution makes the pre-set
option disproportionately likely to stand. Formally, let the chooser realize the
default $j_0$ unless she pays an idiosyncratic switching cost $c_i$ to move,
choosing to switch only when the utility gain exceeds that cost,
$$
\Pr(\text{switch from } j_0 \text{ to } j) = \Pr\!\big(U_{ij} - U_{ij_0} > c_i\big).
$$ {#eq-default}
When $c_i$ is small the default barely matters; when $c_i$ is large—or when the
chooser never engages the comparison at all because attention is itself
costly—the default captures nearly the whole market. Three forces inflate the
effective $c_i$: **inertia** (status-quo bias, an instance of loss aversion in
which moving away from the reference point registers as a loss), **implied
endorsement** (the chooser reads the default as the architect's recommendation),
and **effort** (comprehending and executing a change has real cognitive and
procedural cost). The celebrated cross-country contrast in organ-donor rates—near
universal registration under opt-out regimes, sparse registration under opt-in,
holding stated attitudes roughly constant—is the limiting case in which $c_i$
dominates the modest utility difference between registering and not
[@johnson2003defaults]. @fig-nud-default traces the process by which the pre-set
option becomes the outcome.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-nud-default
%%| fig-cap: "How a default captures the choice. The pre-set option obtains unless the chooser engages the comparison and the utility gain from switching exceeds the switching cost, which inertia, implied endorsement, and effort all inflate."
flowchart TD
  J0["Default j0 pre-set:<br/>obtains if the chooser<br/>does nothing"] --> AT{"Does the chooser engage<br/>the comparison at all?<br/>(attention is costly)"}
  AT -->|"no"| ST["Default stands"]
  AT -->|"yes"| SW{"Utility gain from switching<br/>greater than cost c_i?"}
  SW -->|"no"| ST
  SW -->|"yes"| MV["Chooser switches to j"]
  F1["Inertia:<br/>status-quo bias,<br/>loss aversion"] --> CI["Forces that inflate c_i"]
  F2["Implied endorsement:<br/>default read as the<br/>architect's recommendation"] --> CI
  F3["Effort:<br/>cognitive and<br/>procedural cost"] --> CI
  CI -.-> SW
```

The same mechanism drives the marquee result in household finance: automatic
enrollment in defined-contribution retirement plans raises participation sharply
and persistently, because the inattentive employee inherits the saving rate and
fund the plan sets rather than the one she would choose on reflection. @madrian2001powersuggestio document the magnitude: switching a plan default from opt-in to opt-out raised participation from roughly half to more than four-fifths, with most enrollees then anchored on the default contribution rate and fund. @thaler2004savemore turn the same insight into a designed instrument, pre-committing employees to raise contributions out of future raises. That defaults can
*remedy* under-saving is non-trivial precisely because under-saving is itself
partly a behavioral failure: @Garbinsky_2020 show that many people save too
little not from rational impatience but from a **positive illusion of financial
responsibility**—they believe themselves more financially responsible than the
average person, and that flattering self-view dampens the felt need to save. A
default that raises the saving rate works *with* the grain of what these
consumers would, on reflection, endorse, which is part of why it is defensible on
welfare grounds.

Defaults are not uniformly benign. The identical inertia that lifts retirement
saving also sustains **negative-option** marketing: a free trial that silently
converts to a paid subscription, or a pre-checked add-on at checkout, harvests
the same $c_i$ for the firm's benefit rather than the chooser's. The welfare sign
of a default thus depends entirely on whether the pre-set option is the one the
chooser would choose with full attention—a question the architecture is designed
to prevent her from confronting.

### Framing

A **frame** is a description of options that is logically equivalent across
versions but psychologically distinct. Framing effects are the direct empirical
signature of the reference dependence in prospect theory: because the value
function is defined over *gains and losses* relative to a reference point rather
than over final states, and is steeper for losses than for equivalent gains,
the same outcome described as a loss looms larger than when described as a gain
[@tversky1981; @thaler1985]. Write the chooser's valuation as reference-dependent,
$$
V_j = v\!\big(\mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{r}\big), \qquad
v'(z) > 0,\quad v''(z) < 0 \text{ for } z>0,\quad v'(0^-) > v'(0^+),
$$ {#eq-frame}
where $\mathbf{r}$ is the reference point and the last inequality—the kink at
zero—is **loss aversion**. A frame is an intervention on $\mathbf{r}$: describing
ground beef as "90% lean" sets the reference at the favorable attribute, while
"10% fat" sets it at the unfavorable one, even though the product is identical.
The neoclassical chooser, valuing final states, is invariant to $\mathbf{r}$ and
hence to the frame; the loss-averse chooser is not.

Framing pervades marketing communication. Attribute frames recolor evaluation of
a fixed product; goal frames cast the *same* action as avoiding a loss or
securing a gain, with loss frames typically more motivating for prevention
behaviors. The "buy now, pay later" (BNPL) instrument studied by @maesen2024buy
is, in part, a framing device: splitting a price into interest-free installments
reframes the reference point for the expenditure, and the authors show with
retailer transaction data (in a difference-in-differences design around BNPL
introduction) and three preregistered experiments that the installment frame
*reduces perceived financial constraint and perceived cost and improves felt
budget control*, raising both purchase incidence and basket size relative to
lump-sum payment. The effect is concentrated among smaller-basket and
credit-reliant shoppers—evidence that the frame bites hardest where the
behavioral primitive (here, narrow bracketing of the payment) is strongest, and
a reminder that a frame that "helps" budget control can simultaneously raise
spending in a way the chooser may not, on reflection, endorse.

### Social Proof

A **social-proof** nudge supplies information about what others do, exploiting
the human tendency to treat peers' behavior as evidence about the correct or
acceptable action—a **descriptive norm**. The mechanism adds a term in others'
choices to systematic utility,
$$
V_{ij} = V_0(\mathbf{x}_j, p_j) + \theta\, s_{j} ,
$$ {#eq-social}
where $s_{j}$ is the (perceived) share of relevant others choosing $j$ and
$\theta$ the conformity weight. Two cautions are built into the construct.
First, the *reference group* matters: norms move behavior most when the
comparison others are similar or proximate, so a generic "most people" appeal is
weaker than one keyed to the chooser's own group [@cialdini1990]. Second, a
descriptive norm can **backfire**. Telling people that an undesirable behavior is
common normalizes it, dragging the below-average performer up but pulling the
above-average performer down toward the mean—the *boomerang* effect—which is why
effective normative interventions pair the descriptive norm with an **injunctive**
cue (social approval or disapproval) that protects already-good performers
[@cialdini1990]. The household energy reports that print a neighbor comparison
alongside a smiley face for low users are the canonical field deployment of
exactly this descriptive-plus-injunctive design. @schultz2007constructdestructi first showed why the injunctive component is not decorative: a purely descriptive norm pulls below-average households down as well as above-average households up, and only the added approval signal prevents that boomerang. @allcott2011socialnorms replicates the design at scale across 600,000 households and finds durable reductions of about two percent.

Social proof also operates through observation of others in the moment of
consumption rather than through reported statistics: the mere revealed presence
of other consumers, and the composition of that crowd, shifts evaluations and
choices, a continuity with the brand-evaluation evidence on virtual supporters
discussed in @sec-branding. The lever's power and its fragility share a root:
because it works by transmitting what is *normal*, it is only as good as the
honesty and relevance of the norm it transmits.

### Salience

A **salience** nudge changes which attribute the chooser attends to, without
changing the attribute set or the prices. Limited attention means the chooser
behaves as if maximizing a *distorted* utility that overweights whatever is
perceptually or cognitively prominent. Let attention weights $\omega_k \ge 0$
multiply the attributes,
$$
\hat V_j = \sum_{k} \omega_k\, \beta_k\, x_{jk}, \qquad
\omega_k = \omega_k(\text{salience of attribute } k),
$$ {#eq-salience}
so that a fully attentive chooser has $\omega_k \equiv 1$ and recovers @eq-16-rum,
while an inattentive one sets $\omega_k$ near zero on neglected attributes
(a tax not shown at the shelf, a shrouded fee) and above one on prominent ones
(a bold "sale" tag, a traffic-light nutrition label). A salience nudge is an
intervention on $\omega_k$: posting calorie counts raises the weight on the
health attribute; displaying tax-inclusive prices raises the weight on the
true price. Crucially—and unlike framing—a salience nudge can be welfare-improving
*precisely because* it pushes $\omega_k$ back toward one, undoing a distortion
the chooser would not endorse, rather than introducing a new one.

The clean identification of salience effects comes from settings where the
*information* is unchanged but its *prominence* varies: making an already-disclosed
fee conspicuous, or an already-available calorie figure visible at the point of
choice, changes behavior even though a rational agent had access to the number all
along. Payment form is the canonical demonstration: holding the amount fixed,
@soman2003paymenttranspare shows that more transparent payment mechanisms —
those that make the outflow perceptually vivid — depress subsequent spending, which
is a pure $\omega_k$ intervention on an unchanged budget constraint. The same
machinery explains why a cost labelled a *tax* is resisted more than an identical
cost labelled a fee or a price [@sussman2011taxesdisliked]: the label changes the
weight, not the arithmetic, which makes it a framing effect with genuine
distributional consequences for policy design. Salience is also the lens through which to read "decoy" and assortment
effects in @sec-pricing and @sec-choice-bayesian: adding a dominated option or
reordering a shelf reweights attention across an unchanged menu.

Regulators facing shrouded fees have two tools: a salience intervention that raises
$\omega_k$ on the fee (disclosure), and a restriction that removes the fee from the menu
(a standardized product). Chile's consumer-credit reforms let @kulkarni2026fineprint
separate them, because standardization and disclosure reached small loans together in
2011 and disclosure alone reached all loans a year later (@sec-causal-rd-stacked).
Disclosure cut delinquency by 13.7 percentage points (40%) and default by 98%;
standardization had no effect. Disclosure did not change the terms of the loans
borrowers took, so the salience gain showed up after purchase, in repayment, rather
than in the choice. An evaluation of a disclosure nudge that looks only at the
choice it was meant to inform can therefore miss most of what it does.

## Heterogeneity, Distribution, and the Equity of Nudging {#sec-nudge-heterogeneity}

Because a nudge acts through $\gamma\, d_j(a)$ rather than through preferences,
its effect is intrinsically heterogeneous: it is largest for the choosers whose
behavioral parameters make them most susceptible and smallest for those who would
choose deliberately regardless. This is not a nuisance to be averaged away; it is
the policy-relevant heart of the matter, because it determines *who* a nudge
moves and therefore its distributional consequences.

@Mrkva_2021 establish this directly: choice-architecture interventions—defaults,
attribute ordering, partitioning—have systematically *larger* effects on
consumers with **lower socioeconomic status, lower numeracy, and lower domain
knowledge**. The mechanism is the susceptibility logic above: those with less
knowledge or numerical fluency engage the deliberate comparison less and so
inherit the architecture more. The distributional implication cuts two ways.
A welfare-improving default (auto-enrollment in saving, a healthier cafeteria
arrangement) disproportionately *helps* the disadvantaged and can **narrow** the
gap that arises when the savvy navigate complex choices and the rest default into
bad ones. The very same asymmetry means an exploitative architecture
disproportionately *harms* the disadvantaged. Heterogeneity is thus an
amplifier whose sign is set by the architect's objective, and a nudge's equity
case rests on aligning that objective with the interests of the most susceptible.

This connects to the welfare argument that follows: the standard libertarian
defense—"opting out is free, so no one is worse off"—is weakest exactly where the
nudge is strongest, because the populations least likely to opt out are the
least-resourced. The freedom to opt out is not equally distributed.

Heterogeneity can also split *which* benefits reach whom. @breza2026navigate ran a
field experiment with largely unbanked garment workers in Bangladesh. Wages that had
been paid in cash were instead deposited automatically into a bank or mobile-money
account, an arrangement that works much like a default: the money arrives in the
account unless the worker takes it out. A comparison group received an account but
continued to be paid in cash. Exposure to payroll accounts raised account use and sped
up learning. Workers built trust in the technology, learned to transact without an
agent's help, and avoided the illicit fees that agents commonly charge inexperienced
customers. The effects were concentrated in mobile-money accounts, the newer, more
complex, and less trusted of the two technologies. In the working-paper version
[@breza2020navigatewp], a machine-learning search for heterogeneous effects found that
the savings gains were broad, but the learning-by-doing gains that protect consumers
went mostly to men, to more educated workers, and to those with prior financial
access. The same intervention can therefore be progressive in its direct effect and
regressive in the learning it induces, and an evaluation that reports only the average
savings effect would miss the second distribution entirely.

## Welfare and Ethics {#sec-nudge-welfare}

Evaluating a nudge requires a welfare criterion, and revealed preference cannot
supply one when $\gamma \neq 0$. If the architecture itself moves choice, then the
chosen option is no longer a clean signal of what the chooser values, and the
analyst cannot infer "she chose it, therefore it made her better off." The
behavioral-welfare-economics response is to define welfare relative to the
chooser's preferences as they would be **absent the manipulating frame**—what she
would choose with full attention, no inertia, and a neutral reference point—and
to judge a nudge by whether it moves actual choice toward that **as-if-rational**
benchmark. A nudge that closes the gap between distorted and undistorted choice is
welfare-improving; one that opens it is not. The difficulty, and it is genuine, is
that the undistorted benchmark is partly a construct of the analyst, not an
observable.

Three principles operationalize the criterion and double as design tests. First,
**preserve and cheapen opt-out**: the libertarian half of the program is honored
only if exiting the default carries trivial cost, and—per
@sec-nudge-heterogeneity—trivial *for the least-resourced chooser*, not merely for
the analyst. Second, **publicity**: a nudge is more likely legitimate if the
architect would be willing to defend it openly to those nudged; covert exploitation
of a bias fails this test where transparent information provision passes it. Third,
**interest alignment**: ask whether $d_j(a)$ steers toward the chooser's own ends
(saving, health, accurate prices) or the architect's (subscription revenue,
larger baskets). The BNPL frame in @maesen2024buy is instructive here—it improves
*felt* budget control while raising spending, so its welfare sign depends on
whether the additional purchases are ones the consumer would endorse on reflection
or ones the frame extracts by narrowing attention to the installment.

The adversarial twin of the nudge is the **dark pattern**: a choice-architecture
device engineered to serve the firm at the chooser's expense—pre-checked add-ons,
buried unsubscribe links, drip-priced fees, confirmshaming, manufactured scarcity.
Dark patterns are nudges that fail all three tests at once: opt-out is made
costly, the design would not survive disclosure, and it steers against the
chooser's interest. The privacy literature documents the analogous machinery in
data collection. @adjerid2019choice show that consumers' privacy choices are
malleable to framing and to subtle changes in how options are presented, and that
the same misdirection that depresses privacy-protective choice can be reversed;
@acquisti2012impact demonstrate that the *control* a platform appears to grant
over disclosure is itself a lever—paradoxically, giving people more nominal
control over publication can increase their willingness to disclose sensitive
information, a control-as-nudge that benefits the data collector. These are the
welfare hard cases: architecture that feels empowering while steering against the
chooser's privacy interest.

@fig-welfare summarizes the decision the architect actually faces: not *whether*
to architect—context is unavoidable—but whether the architecture they cannot help
imposing is aimed at the chooser's ends or their own.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-welfare
%%| fig-cap: "Classifying a choice-architecture intervention by its welfare sign. The same formal object—a non-zero behavioral sensitivity to presentation—can be a welfare-improving nudge or an exploitative dark pattern; the three tests separate them."
flowchart TD
    A[Choice architecture<br/>γ·d_j a ≠ 0] --> B{Is opt-out cheap<br/>for the least-resourced chooser?}
    B -- No --> D[Dark pattern]
    B -- Yes --> C{Would the design<br/>survive public disclosure?}
    C -- No --> D
    C -- Yes --> E{Does it steer toward the<br/>chooser's ends or the architect's?}
    E -- Architect's --> D
    E -- Chooser's --> F[Welfare-improving nudge]
    D --> G[Reject / regulate]
    F --> H[Deploy and audit]
```

## Case: Tip Requests and the Tipping-Culture Debate {#sec-nudge-tipping}

Few pieces of choice architecture draw as much public complaint as the tip prompt.
Card readers, self-checkout kiosks, delivery apps, and freelance marketplaces now ask
for a gratuity where none used to be customary, usually with preset buttons between
15% and 30%, and press coverage has reported customers calling the screens
coercive [@kim2026tiprequest]. Critics see the prompt as the dark pattern of
@sec-nudge-welfare: a price increase in disguise, which shifts wage costs onto
customers and collects payment through guilt rather than value. Defenders reply that
a tip is the one charge only willing buyers pay. On that view it is self-selected
price discrimination that keeps posted prices low and rewards effort, and for many
gig workers it is a material share of pay [@azar2020tipping; @kim2026tiprequest].

Underneath the rhetoric the debate turns on two empirical questions, and both map
onto levers from this chapter. Does the wording of the request move behavior, or
only the preset amounts (a default)? And when a prompt raises tips, does the
platform lose future business, so that a tip behaves like a price increase?

**What the default evidence already showed.** @haggag2014defaulttips use a regression
discontinuity in New York City taxi payment screens covering more than 13 million
rides. Suggested tip defaults have a large effect on tip amounts, but higher
suggestions also raise the share of riders who leave no card tip at all. That is the
default lever's opt-out cost made visible. @alexander2021tiprecs randomize tip
recommendations across 94,571 orders from 24,637 customers of an app-based laundry
service. The recommendations shift tip amounts but leave satisfaction ratings,
return frequency, and bill size unchanged. Interface order matters as well: asking
for a rating before the tip lowers tips, because customers feel the rating already
rewarded the provider [@chen2022]. None of this work varied the message itself.

**The experiment.** @kim2026tiprequest ran the first large field experiments on
tip-request wording, on Fiverr, a global freelance-services marketplace where buyer
and seller never meet or speak. After a buyer confirms delivery and rates the gig,
the platform shows a tip request with preset amounts. Before the experiment 8% of
transactions were tipped, and 70% of tips used a preset button. The web experiment
(four weeks from June 10, 2019, persistent randomization at the buyer level) tested
four messages:

- Control: "Would you like to leave a tip to [seller name]?"
- Impersonal reciprocity: "Show your appreciation to your seller by giving a tip."
- Personalized reciprocity: "Leave [seller name] a tip to show your appreciation for a job well done."
- Injunctive norm: "It's customary to leave a tip for the seller's service."

The norm message is injunctive in the sense of @cialdini1990. It states what buyers
ought to do and reports nothing about what most buyers actually do, which would be a
descriptive norm and, since actual tipping was rare, would risk the boomerang
effect described under Social Proof above.

**A confound, and how the authors broke it.** The platform's testing tool allowed only
four cells, and management bundled the two stronger messages with a new
three-default menu ($5/$10/$15 below a $35 order price, 15%/20%/25% above, versus the
old $5/$10 and 20%/30%). As run, the test confounds message with menu. The way out
came from what happened afterwards: when the test ended, every arm reverted to the
control message but kept the three-default menu. Pooling test and posttest periods
gives eight cells, and each message effect is a within-menu contrast. The norm effect
compares norm-plus-three-defaults during the test with the control-plus-three-defaults
cell that the same arm moved into afterwards, and the menu effect compares the control
arm before and after. The design is a regression discontinuity in time layered on a
randomized trial. It requires that tipping respond only to the current treatment, that
the test dates were set by the firm's testing calendar rather than by expected
business, and that nothing else jumps at the boundary. A donut check that drops the
last test week and first posttest week leaves the estimates essentially unchanged.
The authors then ran a clean A/B test of the norm message in the mobile app (October
17 to December 10, 2019, 61,705 transactions), with the same three-default menu in
both arms. @tbl-nud-tipping collects the main estimates.

| Effect on tipping rate (percentage points) | All buyers, first exposure | New buyers, first exposure | Repeat buyers, first exposure | All buyers, all exposures |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Control tipping rate (web) | 14.8% | 14.6% | 14.9% | 10.6% |
| Impersonal reciprocity | +0.4 (n.s.) | +0.8 (n.s.) | +0.3 (n.s.) | 0.0 (n.s.) |
| Personalized reciprocity | +4.6 | +5.3 | +4.4 | +1.5 |
| Injunctive norm | +7.6 | +11.8 | +6.8 | +3.0 |
| Three-default menu (vs. two) | −4.4 | −4.7 | −4.3 | −1.5 |
| App A/B test: control rate | 8.4% | 9.5% | 8.0% | 7.5% |
| App A/B test: injunctive norm | +1.7 | +2.5 | +1.4 | +1.1 |

: Tip-request message and default-menu effects on Fiverr, from @kim2026tiprequest Tables 2 and 3. Linear probability models with buyer-clustered standard errors. Unmarked web estimates are significant at *p* < 0.001; app estimates at *p* < 0.01 or better. "First exposure" is a buyer's first transaction under a given message-and-menu combination. {#tbl-nud-tipping}

Four results bear on the debate. First, wording matters, and the ordering follows
theory. The injunctive norm beat personalized reciprocity, and impersonal reciprocity
did nothing. Naming the seller seems to be what makes a gratitude appeal work, since
it reminds the buyer who earned the thanks. Second, the norm effect is largest for new
buyers, who have the least idea what is customary on the platform. Third, the menu
change *lowered* tipping. Adding a $15 button and replacing the 30% option with 15%
and 25% pulled tips down, so more options are not automatically a stronger nudge.
Fourth, effects grow with order price. In the web test the norm raised first-exposure
tipping by 4.6 points on gigs of $10 or less and by 10.9 points above $60; in the app
the only large effect was above $60. One reading is that a percentage default
loses its pull at high prices, where the tip is expensive enough to be thought
through, and an explicit norm takes over that work.

**Did tips cost the platform demand?** Not detectably, and this is the result that
speaks most directly to the "tips are a price increase" side. In the web experiment,
buyers assigned the norm message placed about 1.5 more orders and spent about $46
more over the period than control buyers, against a base of roughly 4 orders and
$141. The three-default menu reduced orders and spending by similar amounts. In the
cleaner app A/B test the norm message had no significant effect on orders or spending
in either direction. Readers should hold the web demand numbers loosely. A 36% lift in
orders from one sentence on a post-purchase screen is very large, it rests on the
pooled test-posttest identification rather than on the randomized contrast alone, and
the app test did not reproduce it. The defensible conclusion is the weaker one in the
paper's title: raising tips did not reduce demand. That matches what
@alexander2021tiprecs found for tip recommendations.

**What the case does not settle.** Even the best arm left most transactions untipped
(about 22% of new buyers tipped on first exposure), so one sentence does not create a
tipping norm on its own. Only one injunctive message was tested, and the data are from
2019, four years before the 2023 wave of complaints about tip screens that the paper
cites. The study observes
untipped transactions and repeat purchases but not irritation, guilt, or reactance, so
a buyer who kept buying while resenting the prompt counts as no harm. The second
author worked part time for Fiverr as a behavioral scientist from 2018 to 2026. The
paper discloses this and states that the firm had no right to censor findings. Earlier
restaurant studies reviewed in the paper point the other way: an explicit request
lowered tips relative to no request, and surveyed customers reported irritation and
lower intent to return [@kim2026tiprequest]. Those studies changed whether a request
appears; this one changes only its wording once a request is already there.

**Running the three welfare tests.** The tests from @sec-nudge-welfare sort the
debate better than the shouting does. *Cheap opt-out:* declining is one click, and the
authors urge platforms to keep tipping fully discretionary; a screen that makes "no
tip" hard to find fails here, whatever its wording. *Publicity:* "It's customary to
leave a tip" states its appeal openly, whereas a pre-selected tip or a guilt-inducing
layout would not survive disclosure. *Interest alignment* is the hard test. Fiverr
keeps 20% of seller revenue, tips included, so the platform shares in whatever the
prompt raises, and nontippers' welfare is not measured. The absence of a demand
penalty is what separates this prompt from a pure transfer engineered for the
architect. Regulation is already in play. New York City requires delivery apps to
request tips at or before checkout with a default of at least 10%, and the authors
warn that mandating specific defaults or wording without testing could lower workers'
tip income. Given the price-dependent and channel-dependent effects in
@tbl-nud-tipping, that warning is well grounded.

## Identifying a Nudge Effect in the Field {#sec-nudge-identification}

A nudge is a causal claim—$\gamma \neq 0$ for a specific $d_j(a)$—and the gold
standard for recovering $\gamma$ is the randomized field experiment, because
laboratory framing effects routinely shrink or vanish under real stakes,
deliberation, and repetition. The estimand is the average treatment effect of
architecture $a$ on the choice of interest. With chooser $i$ randomized to the
nudge ($T_i=1$) or the status-quo architecture ($T_i=0$), and outcome $Y_i$ (e.g.,
enrollment, basket size, the share choosing the target option),
$$
\tau = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid T_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid T_i = 0],
$$ {#eq-ate}
identified under randomization by the independence of $T_i$ from potential
outcomes. The **estimator** is the difference in means (or a regression of $Y_i$
on $T_i$ with pre-treatment covariates to soak up residual variance); its
**assumptions** are (i) successful randomization, so treatment is orthogonal to
potential outcomes; (ii) the stable-unit-treatment-value assumption (SUTVA)—no
interference between units—which a *social-proof* nudge can threaten precisely
because it operates through peers; and (iii) no differential attrition between
arms. **What breaks identification:** spillovers (the nudged and un-nudged talk,
or share a shelf), non-compliance (the default is overridden administratively),
and outcome measures that capture short-run novelty rather than persistent
behavior. The persistence question is first-order for defaults, whose entire
value rests on inertia *lasting*; a one-week bump that decays is not the same
asset as auto-enrollment that compounds for decades.

Persistence matters for nudges other than defaults too. A real-time prompt is a
salience nudge (@eq-salience) aimed at one decision, and the obvious worry is that
its effect ends with the basket. @gonzalvez2026swapsave test this with "swap and
save" buttons on an online grocery price-comparison platform. The buttons flag a
cheaper alternative while the shopper is choosing, and the authors study the
mineral water category. Shoppers who switched after a prompt were 23.7 percentage
points more likely to choose the alternative again on later visits, and the effect
lasted for up to 10 shopping trips. The authors attribute the persistence to
product discovery rather than to long-run cost savings: the prompt introduced
shoppers to a product they went on to keep buying. This is the state-dependence
problem of @sec-em-week09 in nudge form. A shopper who keeps buying the swapped
product may have learned something from the prompt, or may be the kind of shopper
who would have drifted to it anyway, and a persistence estimate is only as
credible as the design that separates the two.

The paper's online appendix shows how the authors separate them. (The main text
was paywalled when this was written, so the 23.7-point headline comes from the
abstract and everything below from the appendix.) The data are a year (2015) of
item-level purchases on an Israeli price-comparison platform that sits on top of
five online supermarkets, merged with a log of every interaction with the swap
prompt. In mineral water that is 71,433 purchases by 11,337 shoppers across 38
products. Three layers of evidence follow.

1. *Matched event study.* Each shopper who swapped is matched to a shopper who
   bought the same initial product at the same supermarket within 30 days and
   was plausibly never shown the button. That leaves 1,343 treated and 1,762
   control shoppers, compared trip by trip around the swap with what the
   appendix calls a CS DiD, the usual shorthand for @callaway2021did. The
   estimate stays between 20.8 and 27.1 points when the controls are restricted
   to not-yet-treated shoppers, the matching window shrinks to two days, the
   sample is cut to infrequent shoppers, or retailer-by-day fixed effects are
   added. Two placebos come back flat: a fake event three trips before the real
   one, and a swap in cleaning products as the "treatment" for water.
2. *Exposure as an instrument.* Swappers chose to swap, so the authors widen the
   sample to everyone who was shown the button, including shoppers who clicked
   and kept their product and shoppers who never clicked, and instrument
   swapping with exposure (@sec-causal-iv-two-instruments works through both
   instruments). Exposure raises the probability of
   a swap by 36.9 points (first-stage $F = 890$), and the IV estimate of the
   swap's effect on later purchases of the alternative is 21.4 points, close to
   the matched estimate. The exclusion restriction is the weak point, because a
   prompt could work as an advertisement even for shoppers who decline it. The
   authors check this directly. Exposed shoppers who did not swap are no more
   likely than controls to buy the alternative later (coefficient $-0.010$, not
   significant).
3. *Stock-outs as a second instrument.* When a shopper's regular water is out of
   stock, the same button offers in-stock substitutes regardless of price.
   About half of the shoppers who hit a stock-out swap (first stage 53.5
   points, $F = 136$), and the forced trial raises later purchases of the
   substitute by 31.8 points. A trial that has nothing to do with saving money
   persists at least as strongly as one prompted by a lower price.

The third result, together with the appendix's price series, is what supports
"discovery, not savings." Price gaps between the commonly swapped pairs move
around zero through the year, so the alternative is not reliably cheaper on the
next trip, yet shoppers keep buying it. Two measurement choices deserve a
reader's attention. Exposure is inferred for non-clickers (the button was
"likely displayed" if someone else triggered a swap on that product, store, and
day), and the alternative product for anyone who did not swap is imputed as the
most common swap target. Both could blur the instrument, though the first stage
is strong enough that weak identification is not the concern. The design is
also observational throughout: the platform never randomized the button, so the
independence of exposure rests on the argument that day-to-day price movements
make the prompt arrive as good as randomly for a given shopper.

When randomization is infeasible because the nudge is rolled out to everyone at
once, the workhorse is **difference-in-differences** (DiD), exactly the design
@maesen2024buy use around the introduction of BNPL. For unit $i$ in period $t$,
$$
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \delta_t + \beta\, (\text{Post}_t \times \text{Treated}_i)
        + \mathbf{z}_{it}^\top\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \varepsilon_{it},
$$ {#eq-16-did}
where $\alpha_i$ are unit fixed effects, $\delta_t$ time fixed effects, and
$\beta$ the nudge effect. DiD identifies $\beta$ under **parallel trends**:
absent the nudge, treated and control units would have moved in parallel. That
assumption fails if the nudge is rolled out *because* the treated group was
already trending differently (selection on trends), if a contemporaneous shock
hits one group only, or if treatment timing is staggered and effects are
heterogeneous across cohorts—the last a now-well-understood pitfall in
two-way-fixed-effects estimation. The credible applications buttress parallel
trends with pre-period event-study coefficients (flat pre-trends) and placebo
outcomes that the nudge should not move. @fig-nud-ident summarizes the two
identification paths and the assumptions each must defend.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-nud-ident
%%| fig-cap: "Two paths to identifying a nudge effect in the field. Randomization identifies the average treatment effect under randomization integrity, SUTVA, and no differential attrition; a rollout to everyone at once forces difference-in-differences, which substitutes parallel trends defended by flat pre-trends and placebo outcomes. Either way, the outcome that matters is persistence, not a novelty bump."
flowchart TD
  CL["Causal claim: γ ≠ 0 for<br/>a specific architecture d_j(a)"] --> RQ{"Can assignment to the<br/>architecture be randomized?"}
  RQ -->|"yes"| RCT["Randomized field experiment:<br/>ATE by difference in means"]
  RQ -->|"no: rolled out to<br/>everyone at once"| DID["Difference-in-differences<br/>around the rollout"]
  RCT --> RA["Must hold: randomization,<br/>SUTVA, no differential attrition"]
  RA --> RB["Breaks: spillovers (social proof),<br/>overridden defaults,<br/>novelty-only outcomes"]
  DID --> PA["Must hold: parallel trends"]
  PA --> PB["Defend with flat pre-trends<br/>(event study) and<br/>placebo outcomes"]
  RB --> PS["Measure persistence:<br/>a default's value pays<br/>only if inertia endures"]
  PB --> PS
```

The simulation below makes the design concrete and reproducible. We generate a
default nudge with a known true effect, embed realistic heterogeneity (the nudge
bites harder on low-knowledge choosers, per @Mrkva_2021), and recover the
treatment effect by the @eq-ate estimator. @fig-nudge-power reports the resulting
enrollment rates and the sampling distribution of the estimated effect.

```{r nudge-experiment}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-nudge-power
#| fig-cap: "Simulated default-nudge field experiment. Left: enrollment rates under the opt-in (status quo) and opt-out (nudge) architectures, overall and split by domain knowledge. Right: the sampling distribution of the estimated treatment effect across 2,000 replications, centered on the true effect (dashed line)."

set.seed(16)

simulate_nudge_trial <- function(n = 4000,
                                 base_enroll = 0.30,   # opt-in baseline take-up
                                 tau_low = 0.45,       # nudge effect, low-knowledge
                                 tau_high = 0.15) {    # nudge effect, high-knowledge
  # Half the sample is low domain knowledge (more susceptible per Mrkva 2021).
  low_knowledge <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
  treat <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                      # randomized opt-out default
  tau_i <- ifelse(low_knowledge == 1, tau_low, tau_high)
  # Enrollment probability is the baseline plus the (heterogeneous) nudge bump.
  p <- pmin(base_enroll + treat * tau_i, 0.99)
  enroll <- rbinom(n, 1, p)
  data.frame(enroll, treat, low_knowledge)
}

dat <- simulate_nudge_trial()

# Difference-in-means estimator of the ATE (eq-ate).
ate_hat <- mean(dat$enroll[dat$treat == 1]) - mean(dat$enroll[dat$treat == 0])

# Subgroup effects to expose heterogeneity.
sub <- aggregate(enroll ~ treat + low_knowledge, dat, mean)

# Sampling distribution of the estimator across replications.
reps <- replicate(2000, {
  d <- simulate_nudge_trial()
  mean(d$enroll[d$treat == 1]) - mean(d$enroll[d$treat == 0])
})

true_ate <- 0.5 * 0.45 + 0.5 * 0.15   # population-average true effect

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Panel 1: enrollment by architecture and knowledge.
bar_mat <- matrix(sub$enroll[order(sub$low_knowledge, sub$treat)],
                  nrow = 2,
                  dimnames = list(c("opt-in", "opt-out"),
                                  c("high know.", "low know.")))
barplot(bar_mat, beside = TRUE, ylim = c(0, 1),
        col = c("grey70", "steelblue"),
        ylab = "enrollment rate", main = "Take-up by architecture")
legend("topleft", c("opt-in (status quo)", "opt-out (nudge)"),
       fill = c("grey70", "steelblue"), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

# Panel 2: sampling distribution of the estimated ATE.
hist(reps, breaks = 30, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     xlab = expression(hat(tau)), main = "Estimated treatment effect")
abline(v = true_ate, lty = 2, lwd = 2)

par(op)

cat("Estimated ATE (single trial): ", round(ate_hat, 3), "\n")
cat("True population ATE:          ", round(true_ate, 3), "\n")
```

The recovered effect lands on the true population average, and the subgroup panel
reproduces the @Mrkva_2021 pattern: the same default moves low-knowledge choosers
roughly three times as much as high-knowledge ones, the heterogeneity that drives
both the equity case and the exploitation risk. Two practical lessons generalize.
First, power the experiment for the *subgroups* that motivate the policy, not just
the pooled effect, because the distributional claim is usually the point. Second,
measure persistence: re-run the outcome at a horizon long enough to distinguish a
durable behavior change from a novelty response, since a default's value is an
annuity that only pays if the inertia endures.

## Pitfalls and Boundary Conditions

Nudges are neither free nor reliably small, and a disciplined account closes with
where they fail. **Effects decay and are context-bound.** A frame that works in
one population, at one stake level, with one reference point, often shrinks under
real consequences or familiarity; the field-versus-lab gap is the single most
common reason a promising laboratory nudge disappoints at scale, which is why
@sec-nudge-identification insists on field randomization and persistence
measurement rather than one-shot lab demonstrations.

**Nudges interact, sometimes destructively.** Stacking a default, a social-proof
message, and a salience cue is not additive: a descriptive norm can *boomerang*
against above-average performers even as it lifts the rest [@cialdini1990], and a
salience nudge that raises attention to one attribute necessarily lowers the
relative weight on others (@eq-salience), so "more salient labels" can crowd out
the very dimension a second nudge was meant to promote. The architect optimizes a
*system* of weights, not a list of independent levers.

**Reactance and distrust.** A nudge perceived as manipulation can trigger
reactance, reversing the intended effect and eroding trust in the architect—a
risk that scales with how covert the steering is and that the publicity test in
@sec-nudge-welfare is designed to forestall. **Crowding-out of intrinsic
motivation** is the subtler cousin: a nudge that does the deliberating *for* the
chooser may atrophy the capacity to choose well unaided, a cost invisible in the
short-run outcome metric but real over a consumer's lifetime of decisions. The
same reversal reaches explicit incentives, not just presentation: in a natural
field experiment, surprise bonuses *lowered* subsequent effort, the payment read
as a signal that the employer was already satisfied rather than a gift to be
reciprocated [@bogliacino2026gifts]—a reminder that an intervention's effect turns
on the meaning the recipient assigns it, not on its size or sign alone.

A long field test shows what separates a small reward that helps from one that
backfires. Theory allows either: a token payment can lower effort below no payment at
all [@gneezy2000payenough]. @bruers2026plasma randomized twelve Red Cross-Flanders
donation centers to three arms. In the control arm nothing changed. In the second, the
monthly newsletter stated the thank-you coupons donors already received: one coupon,
worth about €1.50, for a blood donation and two for plasma. The third arm got the same
newsletter and, for six months, a third coupon for plasma. The reminder alone raised
plasma donations by 4.6% over nine months, but it faded as it was repeated, a decay
that a one-shot measurement would miss (@sec-nudge-identification). The extra coupon
raised plasma donations by a further 7.1%. That effect grew while the coupon was
offered and disappeared once it was withdrawn. The dissertation chapter that first
reported the experiment finds no drop below the pre-reward level, which is the backlash
crowding-out would predict [@bruers2024thesis]. The reward also lowered blood donations
at the same centers by 3.3%, so part of the gain was donors switching between two
prosocial acts. Earlier work on blood drives found incentives pulling donors away from
nearby drives that offered none [@lacetera2012blood]. Here the displacement runs across
products, which an evaluation that counts only the rewarded behavior cannot see. Survey
evidence in the paper suggests that small rewards act as signals of increased need or
as gifts that call for reciprocity. That is the same channel as the surprise bonus
above: the effect depends on what recipients take the reward to mean, but here the
sign is positive. A non-cash gift may also avoid the exchange norms that monetary
tokens activate [@yin2020], although the experiment does not compare coupons with cash.
@sec-sw-emb-plasma reads the paper as a model for framing a simple field experiment.


**Removing friction is not always the right move.** Sludge analysis treats each added
step as a cost [@thaler2018sludge], which is correct when the goal is uptake.
@dykstra2026buyin test the case where the goal is use. When the Oregon Department of
Transportation moved its carpool platform to a new vendor in 2019, they randomized
27,227 users who had been inactive for six months to two migration emails. In the
low-effort arm the account had already been moved and the user only reset a
password. In the high-effort arm the user rebuilt the account over three pages,
re-entering name, home and work zip codes, and employer
[@dykstra2024buyinregistry]. Nothing else differed: both arms then had to search
for matches and log trips the same way. The harder path lowered sign-ups from 5.1%
to 3.8% (694 against 511 people), a 25% drop. Over four months, though, the
high-effort arm logged 0.057 more carpool trips per week per person assigned, on a
low-effort mean of 0.034, and 5,106 trips in total against 4,311.

The design point is why an intent-to-treat (ITT) gain rules out pure selection.
Assignment to the hard path can only remove the "complacent" users who would have
signed up only if it were easy, and a removed user contributes zero trips, never a
negative number. If the hard path merely filtered out less committed people, total
trips in that arm could only stay the same or fall. They rose, so the users who
signed up anyway must have carpooled more than they would have after an easy
sign-up. A worst-case bound points the same way. Dropping the 25% least active
low-effort sign-ups, the share the hard path screened out, shrinks the effect among
sign-ups from 1.73 to 1.51 extra trips per week, so selection accounts for some of
the effect but not most of it. The effect has limits. At eight months it was about
a fifth of its four-month size, and the effect on miles was no longer significant.
The October wave alone (10,191 users) was not significant. And the AEA registration
was filed after data collection, with the hypotheses fixed earlier in the IRB
protocol.

A second experiment, preregistered on Amazon Mechanical Turk with 496 workers
[@oflaherty2025buyinregistry], made workers who wanted a next-day round of an
unpleasant transcription task first answer a 15-question survey about that kind of
work. Sign-ups fell only slightly (80.8% to 76.8%, not significant), returns rose
from 36.4% to 50.0%, and the effortful arm transcribed 8,438 letters correctly
against 5,598. Cross-randomized arms suggest where the effect comes from. A next-day
reminder email neither raised returns nor reduced the effort effect, which counts
against a memory channel and leaves perceived value as the authors' preferred
reading, though they do not isolate it. Donating the earnings to charity lowered
returns by 23 points without changing the effort effect, so the effect does not
depend on the task being prosocial.

Three lessons follow for the architect. First, the outcome decides the sign of the
effect. A team that scored the carpool test on sign-ups would have dropped the arm
that produced the most trips, the same uptake-versus-persistence gap that
@sec-nudge-identification warns about. Second, friction is not one quantity with a
fixed welfare sign: the authors expect a gain only when the follow-through behavior
is voluntary and ongoing and the added step is modest and tied to the goal. Paperwork
that only filters people out is the sludge case. Third, the net effect depends on
the population. The hard path cost 25% of sign-ups in the field and 5% online, and a
population with more complacent users could lose more participation than the
remaining users' extra effort makes up.

Finally, the **measurement of welfare remains the binding constraint.** Because
the undistorted benchmark in @sec-nudge-welfare is partly constructed by the
analyst, two honest researchers can disagree about a nudge's sign even given the
same effect estimate. The responsible posture is to make the welfare model
explicit—state the assumed reference preference, justify it, and report the effect
on the susceptible subgroups separately—rather than to let an impressive average
treatment effect stand in for a welfare argument it cannot make.

## Key Takeaways

- A **nudge** changes behavior through the choice architecture
  ($\gamma\, d_j(a)$ in @eq-nudge) without altering the menu or the economic
  terms; under the neoclassical axioms $\gamma = 0$, so every nudge is a claim
  that presentation matters where a rational agent would ignore it.
- The four core levers map onto distinct behavioral primitives: **defaults**
  exploit inertia (@eq-default), **framing** exploits reference dependence and
  loss aversion (@eq-frame), **social proof** exploits descriptive norms
  (@eq-social), and **salience** exploits limited attention (@eq-salience).
- Nudge effects are **intrinsically heterogeneous** and largest for low-SES,
  low-numeracy, low-knowledge choosers [@Mrkva_2021], so a nudge's distributional
  sign is set by the architect's objective—amplifying help or harm alike.
- **Welfare cannot be read off revealed choice** when $\gamma \neq 0$; legitimacy
  turns on cheap opt-out, surviving public disclosure, and alignment with the
  chooser's own ends. **Dark patterns** are nudges that fail all three.
- Identifying $\gamma$ in the field means a randomized experiment (@eq-ate) or a
  parallel-trends DiD (@eq-16-did), powered for the susceptible subgroups and
  measured for **persistence**, not novelty.

## Further Reading

The reference-dependence and heuristics foundations are @kahneman1979prospect,
@tversky1974, @tversky1981, @tverskykahneman1991loss, and @thaler1985; salience and
present bias are @bordalo2013salience and @laibson1997hyperbolic; the
normative social-influence machinery is @cialdini1990 and @goldstein2008norms. The
choice-architecture program rests on the default evidence of @johnson2003defaults,
the scale evidence of @benartzi2017nudging, and the sludge counterpoint of
@thaler2018sludge (the *Nudge* monograph of Thaler and Sunstein states the
libertarian-paternalism framing in full). For frontier field and behavioral evidence weave the
saving-illusion result of @Garbinsky_2020, the choice-architecture-and-inequity
result of @Mrkva_2021, the BNPL framing evidence of @maesen2024buy, and the
privacy choice-architecture work of @adjerid2019choice and @acquisti2012impact.
For tipping as choice architecture, read @azar2020tipping for the economics,
@haggag2014defaulttips and @alexander2021tiprecs on preset tips, and
@kim2026tiprequest on request wording (@sec-nudge-tipping).
The construct connects forward to assortment and decoy effects in
@sec-choice-bayesian, price framing in @sec-pricing, and the social-evaluation
evidence in @sec-branding.
